title: Methodus generalior numeros quosvis satis grandes perscrutandi utrum sint primi necne?

deep.reconstruction:
Context (E719, Methodus generalior...): Euler's primality test uses 'numeri idonei' (convenient numbers) αβ. If N = α a² + β b² with αβ idoneal, gcd conditions satisfied, and this is the only representation of N in the form αx² + βy², then N is prime. A second representation reveals a factor. On the previous page Euler writes α = μν, sets y + b = μp and y − b = νq, so that y² − b² = αpq. The condition α a² − β(y² − b²) = α x² then becomes a² − βpq = x².

This page, §41: eliminate y to get the linear Diophantine condition 2b = μp − νq. Take a convergent-type fraction m/n ≈ μ/ν with mν − nμ = 1. Then a particular solution is p0 = −2nb, q0 = −2mb, and the general solution is p = νs − 2nb, q = μs − 2mb with s ∈ Z. The problem reduces to finding integers s for which

a² − S(s) is a perfect square, where S(s) = β(νs − 2nb)(μs − 2mb).

S is a quadratic in s with positive leading coefficient βμν. So only finitely many s (in both directions from 0) give S ≤ a², and the search is finite.

§42: tabulate S(0) = 4βmn b², S(±1) = β(ν ∓ 2nb)(μ ∓ 2mb), and so on. Expanding, S(s) = β[μν s² − 2b(mν + nμ)s + 4mn b²]. The first differences are S(k) − S(k−1) = β((2k−1)μν ∓ 2b(mν + nμ)), so the second difference is constant, 2βμν.

§43: starting from a² − S(0), subtract the successive differences, in both directions of s. Check each remainder for being a square, and stop when the remainders become negative. If no square appears, N is declared prime. If x² appears at some s, then y = νq + b = μνs − b(2mν − 1) = μνs − b(mν + nμ), using mν = 1 + nμ, and the second representation (x, y) is obtained.

§44: halve the work by sorting s into residue classes mod 4. For even s, one of the classes s ≡ 0, 2 (mod 4) usually forces S to be ≡ 2 (mod 4) (impariter par), which excludes it. For odd s, one of s ≡ ±1 (mod 4) is excluded because odd squares are ≡ 1 (mod 8). In effect this is a finite-difference quadratic-sieve search for squares, a variant of Fermat's difference-of-squares idea adapted to binary quadratic forms with idoneal discriminant.
errors: The relation obtained by eliminating y must be 2b = μp − νq (from μp = y + b, νq = y − b). The transcribed 'νp − μq' is inconsistent with the parametrization p = νs − 2nb, q = μs − 2mb. It also contradicts the worked example on p. 28, where μ = 10, ν = 4 gives b = 5p − 2q. Whether the printed text itself has the slip is hard to read in the scan.

The 'certe pro primo' conclusion tacitly requires extra hypotheses that Euler states only elsewhere: αβ idoneal, gcd(N, αβ) = 1, gcd(αa, βb) = 1, and attention to non-primitive representations. Otherwise the uniqueness criterion can fail.
The mod-4 / mod-8 exclusion in §44 is only heuristic ('plerumque'). Euler acknowledges this himself, and whether a class is excluded depends on the parities of a, b, β, μ, ν.
Euler reuses the letter n in s = 4n, 4n+2, 4n±1 in §44 while n already denotes the denominator in m/n. This is a harmless notational clash.

Minor point: Euler says each factorization α = μν must be examined separately. Swapping μ and ν only replaces y by −y, so unordered factorizations suffice. The text does not say this explicitly but is not wrong.

ideas.what: Primality test by uniqueness of representation N = αa² + βb² with αβ idoneal; a second representation yields factors
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (c. 1778 onward; discussed by Gauss, Weil)
ideas.where_published: E708, E715, E718, E719 and related papers in Nova Acta; discussed in Weil, Number Theory: An Approach through History

ideas.what: Solving μp − νq = 2b via a fraction m/n with mν − nμ = 1 to parametrize all (p, q) by one integer s
ideas.modern_name: Bezout / continued-fraction solution of a linear Diophantine equation
ideas.where_published: Euler's Algebra (E387/388) and many number-theory papers

ideas.what: Searching for squares among a² − S(s), with S quadratic in s, by subtracting successive first differences (constant second difference)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Fermat (difference of squares); Euler's own tabular methods
ideas.where_published: Same method in E699/E715/E718 and in the worked examples of E719 itself

ideas.what: Halving the search by excluding residue classes of s mod 4, using that odd squares are ≡ 1 mod 8 and that numbers ≡ 2 mod 4 are not differences of squares
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones §§ on exclusion), later Lehmer sieves
ideas.where_published: Similar exclusion remarks in Euler's factoring papers (e.g., E228, E699)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful but standard algorithmic step in Euler's well-documented idoneal-number primality method. The linear parametrization and difference table are routine, and the mod-8 exclusion is a known Euler/Gauss device. Nothing here appears to be absent from the literature.
transcription_corrections: '2b = νp − μq' should read '2b = μp − νq' (as required by y+b = μp, y−b = νq and confirmed by b = 5p − 2q on p. 28).
'an dico usquam' is likely 'an, inquam, usquam' or a similar emphatic phrase. The meaning is 'whether anywhere a square can result'.
In §43, 'primo termino minuto' means subtract from aa already diminished by the first term S(0) = 4βmnbb, i.e. from aa − 4βmnbb (cf. p. 28, 'a numero aa − 26bb').
In §44, the letter n in s = 4n, 4n+2, 4n±1 is a generic integer, not the n of m/n.
